claims.text: High-energy ball milling followed by spark plasma sintering can produce a large-scale RHEA–Cu composite.
CALPHAD-based multicomponent free-energy modeling can optimize the processing window for the proposed RHEA–Cu powder-metallurgy route.
The proposed route will yield a stable and uniform RHEA–Cu microstructure despite positive Cu–refractory mixing enthalpy.
The initial RHEA-constituent and Cu powder mixture is phase separated or has limited interfacial contact.
High-energy ball milling promotes uniform mixing of the RHEA constituents and Cu.
High-energy ball milling introduces defects that facilitate alloying.
Rapid spark-plasma-sintering consolidation limits the time available for diffusion-driven phase separation.
An optimized thermodynamic processing window can suppress segregation effects associated with positive Cu–refractory mixing enthalpy.
The processing route will create a refined, finely dispersed microstructure with minimized phase segregation at the RHEA–Cu interface.
The processing route will enhance interfacial coherence between the RHEA and Cu.
The resulting RHEA–Cu composite will be dense and microstructurally uniform.
The resulting RHEA–Cu composite will exhibit reduced elemental segregation and improved interfacial stability.
The resulting RHEA–Cu composite will have enhanced resistance to high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
Conventional melting or slower sintering generally causes segregation and unstable microstructures in RHEA–Cu materials because of positive mixing enthalpy.
The hypothesis is limited to compositions for which the free-energy model accurately represents Cu–refractory interactions and to processing conditions within the optimized regime.
Extrapolation to substantially different compositions or processing scales may require additional validation.
Free-energy-model predictions may be imprecise under rapid processing conditions.
Scale-up may produce residual segregation or spatial variations in microstructural uniformity.
